source: Generated by scripts/sync-release-snapshot.ts from registry.npmjs.org and the GitHub releases API. Do not edit by hand.

releases.notes: A battery was drawn the wrong way round. The long plate marks a battery's positive terminal, but the symbol drew it beside the negative port, so every battery showed the opposite polarity to the one its terminals carry, in every orientation. A reader following the drawing would connect it backwards. The two plates have changed places, so the long plate now sits on positive. Only the drawing changes: both plates keep their extents, so bounds, ports and routes are untouched. Of the 270 corpus documents, only variant/source/battery draws different bytes, and its layout and diagnostics digest is unchanged. Found by the CircuiTikZ converter (schemd/circuitikz#2). Source polarity marks pointed at neither terminal.

1.3 states what every component kind accepts, as data. Nothing about compiling changes: the 270-document corpus is byte-identical to 1.2.0, and the compile path and the package entry are the same bytes. @schemd/core/schema describes every kind's options. An editor that wanted to list what ground or mux accepts had to read the parser or copy a table by hand, and a copied table drifts. SCHEMATICCOMPONENTSCHEMAS gives each of the compiler's kinds its family and its options, each with a type and what that type allows: enum, with its values and default; integer or number, with its range, its default, and any default that depends on the kind's type (a full adder's three inputs, a demultiplexer's two outputs); text, with its length bounds; pins, with the most pins per side, the pattern a pin name must match and the names it may not take; rows, with the most rows and the longest row.

1.2 lets a part be declared without a label. Every 1.1 document compiles to the same bytes: the 270-document corpus is byte-identical to 1.1.0. The quoted label is optional. resistor:R1 at (240, 80) #amber and junction:J1 right-of R1 by 100 #slate are now declarations; before, a part needed a label, so authors and tools repeated the ID (junction:J1 "J1") and the designator was drawn twice. A part without a label draws its designator alone: no label row is drawn, and the router no longer keeps wires clear of one; its accessible name in full mode is R1, resistor, fixed, without an empty field; its AST and netlist label is the empty string, and describeSchematic names it by its ID; parseSchematicSvg reads it back without a label, and the recovered source recompiles to the same parts. An empty quoted label, "", is still rejected.

1.1 lets a part take its height from its wires. Every 1.0 document compiles to the same bytes: the 270-document corpus is byte-identical to 1.0.2, and fitting happens only where a document asks for it. fit=wires lines a part's terminals up with the wires that reach them. A block with several terminals on a side has a fixed pitch, so wires bent to meet it: two qubit rails 120 units apart jogged in to a CNOT whose rails are 18 apart, and out again, and three Hadamard outputs fed an oracle block through two 100-unit detours. On a part declared fit=wires, each terminal takes the height of the terminal wired to it, the part is centred between them, and a block's body grows to hold them, so the wires arrive straight. Across the Bell, teleportation, Grover, error-correction and phase-kickback circuits on the schemd site, 20 bends and 13 diagonal wire segments become none.

A part placed against a declaration that failed is no longer told that declaration does not exist. When a declaration's own line failed — an unknown option, say — anything placed relative to it was reported as referencing a part "the document never declares", which sent the author to a line that was fine. It is now left unplaced without a second diagnostic, as 1.0 already did for everything that depends on a failed placement. resolvePlacements takes the ids that already failed as an optional fifth argument. Found while writing the 1.0 documentation's diagnostics page. A broken placement no longer hides a mistyped terminal elsewhere. diagnoseSchematic stopped as soon as any relative placement failed, so a connection to a terminal that does not exist went unreported until the placement was fixed.

No changes from 1.0.0. This version was tagged before the fixes meant for it were merged, so its package is 1.0.0's code under a new version number; those fixes shipped as 1.0.2. Upgrading from 1.0.0 to 1.0.1 changes nothing.

1.0 is a rebuild of the compiler's core behind the same language and the same API. The language is read exactly as before — the 0.8 declaration patterns are the front end — and of the corpus's 54 rejections under 0.8, 52 are byte-identical in 1.0. Drawings change, because the router is new, and three corpus documents change outcome; each is listed under Changed. Wires are routed by net, and a multi-terminal net is always a tree. Connections that share a terminal are grown as one tree: the first runs terminal to terminal, every later one leaves the nearest copper the net already has, and every junction gets a dot. A junction is held two pitches off any pin, and a tree never meets four ways at one point. trunk is still parsed, validated and recorded as connection.trunk, but the drawing no longer depends on it — a net without it is drawn the same tree.

trunk draws a multi-terminal net as a tree. A net reaching four terminals used to be three wires that each ran back to the shared pin — stacked on one another where the router reused a channel, and meeting at T-junctions with no dot, which a reader cannot tell from a crossing. Mark a connection [ortho trunk] and it leaves the nearest copper its net already has instead of its own terminal, with a junction dot where it joins. Every point on a net is the same electrical node, so the netlist, verifyNetlist, describeSchematic and the source map are unchanged; only the drawing is. Which end joins the net is decided by the source text. A branch needs exactly one terminal already wired by a connection declared above it; that end becomes a tap and the other is the terminal the branch reaches.

A reversal bus routes at thirty-two wires, up from twelve. When rip-up spends its whole budget the traces are no longer retried again in a different order — the bundle is laid out as a set. Every trace takes the same five-segment dogleg and they differ only in where each turns: rank decides an outbound column stepping inward from the source, an inbound column stepping inward from the target, and a row through the middle band. Assignment is made for the bundle at once, which is the thing reordering structurally cannot do. routing.nudged reports whether a document needed that path. False for everything that routed greedily, which is every document that compiled before this release. It is a rescue, not a replacement. It runs only after the retry budget is exhausted, so a document that compiles today reaches the same routes through the same code — all 261 corpus drawings are byte-identical.

snapshotSchematic — a text digest of a diagram's geometry, at @schemd/core/snapshot. Every component rectangle and every trace vertex, rounded to the three decimals the SVG writer emits, in source order, behind a schemd-snapshot 1 version line. Committed as a fixture, a routing change now shows up in a pull request as the handful of coordinates that moved rather than as a red blob in an image diff. It does not replace the Chromium goldens: nothing here can tell you an arrowhead went missing, which is why tests/visual keeps the cases that need a renderer. parseSchematicSvg — reading a compiled diagram back into declarations, at @schemd/core/decompile. full mode already stamps each node group with its id, kind, label, line and orientation, positions it with a translate and paints it with a colour token; each wire group carries its endpoints, net, signal domain and bus width.

Relative placement. A declaration can state where it sits instead of computing it: resistor:R1 "1 kΩ" right-of VIN by 190 #amber. Six relations — right-of, left-of, above, below, aligned-x with, aligned-y with — each taking a component or one of its terminals, and the four directions taking an optional by distance. at (x, y) is untouched, the two forms mix freely, and a document that uses only coordinates compiles to the bytes it always did. Directions measure from the referenced body, so by 190 is 190 units of clear space between facing edges. An axis no relation sets is inherited from the first reference, so right-of A means beside A and level with it; an alignment overrides that. It is a lowering pass, not a layout engine. Relations resolve to one at (x, y) before the AST is finished, so the netlist, design rules, source map, and renderer never learn relative placement exists.

Every connection that declares a closed endpoint marker paints one. SVG resolves marker-start at the first vertex of a path element and marker-end at its last — not once per subpath — so the compound trace that default and embedded-css output emit showed a single arrowhead however many wires shared a batch. Three [arrow] connections in one colour produced three lines and one arrow. Connections carrying arrow, dot, or diamond-filled now keep a path to themselves; unmarked traces still compound, and open markers still travel on their own carrier. Every marker fixture in the suite happened to give each wire a distinct colour, which put every wire in a batch of its own and hid the defect from the goldens. A reversal bus routes.

Geometry diagnostics say how to fix the diagram, not only what is wrong with it. An overlap now reports the amount and a coordinate that clears it — R2 overlaps R1 by 44 units horizontally; move R2 to x = 284, or use a UML container — expressed in the at (x, y) origin the author types rather than the derived body rectangle. The advice follows the axis the author already used to separate the pair, so two parts side by side move apart sideways instead of being stacked because that happened to be eight units cheaper. Out-of-bounds diagnostics name the offending coordinate and the range it must fall in. A body that escapes the canvas after layout reports the overhang and an origin that would contain it, and notes that widening the fence is also an answer. The README carries a standing statement of limitations and operational risks.

@schemd/core/netlist and @schemd/core/describe are importable. Both modules shipped in the tarball with no entry in the package exports map, so import '@schemd/core/netlist' failed with ERRPACKAGEPATHNOTEXPORTED while dist/netlist.js sat there unused — the netlist subpath since it was announced in 0.3.4, the describe subpath since 0.3.6. Nothing caught either, because every test imports from src, where subpaths do not exist. A packaging test now decides, in one place, which source modules are public: every one of them must have a subpath, every subpath must resolve to the module it names, and no subpath may point at a module that is not there. Removing an entry fails the suite.

Diagrams can describe themselves. describeSchematic and describeNetlist derive a deterministic account of a document from its connectivity — scale and signal domain in one sentence fit for an alt attribute, an inventory grouped by kind, and one sentence per net naming the terminals it ties. Labels are flattened through the same mathLabelText the renderer uses, so V{in} is spoken as Vin and 1 k\Omega as 1 kΩ. The description states only what the netlist proves: it does not name circuit archetypes, because recognising an intent the source never declared produces a confident wrong label, which is worse for a screen-reader user than an accurate structural one. The module is deliberately absent from the package entry, so neither size budget moves and a host that only compiles carries no prose generation.

The router's spatial hash addresses both axes. Cells were keyed on x alone, so a single column held every obstacle stacked along it and a short segment paid the participation predicate and a slab test once per row — the quadratic term in routing a tall document. Obstacle and wire cells are now keyed on column and row, with a y-span rejection ahead of the exact predicates. Dense 16x16 routing drops from 7.7 ms to 4.1 ms, and a 512-component chain — one connection per component, the shape that provoked the old behaviour — from 40.4 ms to 16.3 ms. Output is byte-identical. Router lane candidates are gathered without intermediate arrays. Each list was built by spreading a two-element array per obstacle into a set; obstacle bounds are now added to the set directly.

Connectivity is now a first-class artifact. buildNetlist returns the nodes, nets, and edges behind a validated document, verifyNetlist runs deterministic design rules over that model, and inspectSchematic does both in one call. Seven rules ship: shorted supply rails, conflicting bus widths, mixed signal domains, unconnected components, duplicate connections, contended digital drivers, and disconnected subcircuits. Diagnostics carry a stable code, a severity, the subjects involved, and the source line wherever a declaration owns the fault. SCHEMATICRULES publishes the rule catalogue — code, severity, and summary — so hosts can document or filter checks without hard-coding strings. Correction (0.3.7): the module was intended to be reachable as @schemd/core/netlist, but the required package export was missing until 0.3.7. Consumers of 0.3.4 through 0.3.6 cannot import that subpath.

cnot is now an intrinsic two-track controlled-X with continuous control and target rails. Canonical in1/out1 and in2/out2 ports compose directly with quantum wires; legacy in, out, control, and target endpoint spellings remain valid. A Chromium golden locks the two-rail CNOT geometry and its reversed horizontal orientation.

Signal connections now resolve to first-class net topology. Exact shared terminals and junction branches join implicitly, net=NAME joins disconnected segments explicitly, unnamed nets receive deterministic $N identities, and every net enforces one signal-domain/width contract. Straight, cubic Bézier, and orthogonal routes now share one collision policy across component bodies, transformed endpoint markers, and topology-aware wire contacts. Separate nets may meet only at bridgeable perpendicular orthogonal crossings. Physical-body overlap detection rejects accidental node collisions while preserving edge contact, UML semantic containment, and lifeline activation/execution/destruction overlays. The validator uses an x-ordered, lazily expired y-bucket sweep and includes a 240-body adversarial regression.

Orthogonal routing no longer fails diagrams whose components sit closer than twice the 12-unit clearance margin. The post-routing guard now rejects only physical body clips; escape stubs may legitimately pass through a neighbor's clearance ring, so densely packed parallel wires route as straight traces instead of throwing Orthogonal route intersects … after routing. Empty qgate detail rows (parameter="", phase="", matrix="") no longer reserve blank text space: layout and renderer now agree that empty details are absent, so such gates keep the canonical shared quantum shell. embedded-css output no longer emits keyboard-focusable component and wire groups beneath its role="img" root, which flattened them for assistive technology while leaving unlabeled tab stops.

Exact quarter-turn component orientation through orientation=right|down|left|up, including rotated ports, outward normals, AABBs, text extents, obstacle routing, and four-turn identity. Electrical sources, native junctions/test points/connectors, power symbols, switch and protection families, amplifiers, resonators, meters, loads, expanded passive/diode/transistor variants, and side-aware IC orientation. Digital buffers, logic states, clocks, latches/flip-flops, mux/demux blocks, encoders, decoders, registers, counters, half/full adders, comparators, and bus primitives. Named and parameterized quantum gates, preparation/reset/measurement, control and swap structures, generalized controlled gates, barriers/delays, and classical result nodes.
Last 0.2.x release. Historical documentation remains at the official 0.2.1 route.
